questions.stem: You turn on App Service built-in authentication for the orders API with "Require authentication". What does that guarantee about a request for /api/orders/7?

options.text: Only the customer who owns order 7 can read it
Only callers with an admin role can read it
Only signed-in callers reach your code; which orders each one may read is still up to your code
Nothing, until a web application firewall is added

questions.stem: Why doesn't tightening CORS, on its own, protect the orders API?

options.text: CORS only tells browsers which other websites may read responses; a script or curl ignores it
CORS only applies to plain HTTP, not HTTPS
App Service ignores CORS settings on Linux
CORS is only checked on POST requests

questions.stem: For the orders API, why is "HTTP 401 Unauthorized" a better response to unauthenticated requests than a redirect to the sign-in page?

options.text: A 401 is cached, so it's faster
A redirect sends the order data along with it
HTTPS requires a 401
API clients aren't browsers: a redirect to a login page breaks them, while a 401 tells them to get a token

questions.stem: The portal's debug page showed no passwords. Why is it still a finding?

options.text: It isn't a finding if no passwords are shown
It reveals internals (build, feature flags, internal endpoints, tokens) that help an attacker, and "temporary" pages get forgotten
It uses CPU minutes on the Free plan
Debug pages bypass HTTPS

questions.stem: The apps' publishing passwords are long and random. Why turn basic-auth publishing off anyway?

options.text: They're long-lived shared credentials, not tied to a person, with no MFA or Conditional Access; Entra tokens are short-lived and tied to an identity
Basic auth makes deployments slower
Leaving it on disables HTTPS
There's no reason if the passwords are strong

questions.stem: httpsOnly already redirects HTTP to HTTPS. What does the Strict-Transport-Security header add?

options.text: It encrypts the redirect itself
It replaces the TLS certificate
After the first visit, the browser refuses plain HTTP to the site, so a later http:// request can't be intercepted before the redirect
Nothing; it only matters for APIs

questions.stem: Would changing order numbers from 1, 2, 3 to random GUIDs fix the orders flaw?

options.text: Yes: nobody can guess a GUID
No: guessing gets harder, but any leaked or shared ID still works; the fix is checking the order belongs to the caller
Yes, as long as the API also requires HTTPS
Only if CORS is also restricted

questions.stem: Your code reads the X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-ID header to know who is calling. When can you trust it?

options.text: Always: browsers can't set custom headers
Only over HTTP/2
Only when CORS is restricted to your own origin
Only when App Service built-in authentication is in front of the app; without it, anyone can send that header
